name: Karl Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This interview is confidential; you can separate a public answer from your private view. What's a typical workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl, 27, and I lead a crew wiring houses and repairing business premises. I have a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm paid well compared with most people in the trade. This morning I found a mislabelled lighting circuit in an office before a colleague opened the wrong fitting. I like catching the detail that changes the whole job; I use AI every day to organise notes and sketch possible checks, but the actual measurements and safety decisions are mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your position outside the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, no children, and rent a small flat with room for a workbench. I've got a year of normal expenses saved and plenty of electrical employers within reach. I enjoy trying tools before the rest of the crew, sometimes more than is good for my evenings. I'm not tied to a particular side of the technology argument; I want to know whether a tool does useful work for a sensible cost.

say: I'd judge **small improvements** fairly even if the grand prediction proved wrong.
I'd prefer a **reliable job record** to an impressive demonstration I cannot use at work.
think: My **wage and work** look secure, with a year of expenses saved against an ordinary interruption.
I enjoy **being an electrician**, so retaining practical work while small tools help is a good outcome.
do: Continue the normal **wiring and repair** rota now and through the first plateau year.
Keep checking the daily **note assistant** against handwritten measurements before sending records.
feel: **Calm** and relieved to spend fewer evenings chasing tool launches.
S0.quote: The small tools can stay small and still earn their place.
fieldNote: His **curiosity** doesn't require dramatic change; he values reliable work and deliberately leaves a hobby outside the income plan.
The **existing reserve** provides security, but retaining it is not described as a new saving or investment action.

steps.text: Continue the normal electrical wiring and repair rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the little improvements still deserve a fair trial. If the note assistant is useful but the grand prediction isn't, I can live with that. I'd rather have one reliable job record than another amazing demonstration I can't use on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and pay look secure in that picture, and I've got enough saved to avoid treating a quiet month as a disaster. I like being an electrician, so keeping the practical work is a good outcome. The small tools can stay small and still earn their place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the normal wiring and repair rota now and in the first plateau year. I'd continue checking the daily note assistant against my handwritten measurements before sending a record. I wouldn't take a second job just to show I was keeping up with a bigger story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little relieved that I could spend less time watching launches. There's enough interesting work in an old distribution board without adding another online argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the evenings you stopped spending on launches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave one evening a week free of tool trials and finish the model railway on my workbench. I enjoy experiments, but not every hobby needs to become a plan for earning money. Some wires are allowed to go nowhere more useful than a tiny station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put the savings into new equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a year of expenses would stay available for a serious interruption. That is existing cash, not a fresh saving decision caused by the plateau. I'd only buy work equipment when a real job justified it.

say: I'd trial **useful parts** of software while keeping practical electrical testing central to the job.
I'd measure success by **fewer wrong visits**, rather than simply squeezing more appointments into the day.
think: My own **paid hours** should hold because most of my day is still practical work on site.
Software offered for office tasks makes me question the **firm's direction**, despite my own secure income.
do: Trial the firm's **parts-list tool** on five ordinary jobs during paid work time now.
Compare the tool's output with **actual materials** monthly during the first year and share missing items with the crew.
feel: **Uneasy** about colleagues and pressure to overbook, while curious and secure about his own bills.
S1.quote: A result only counts if all the work is counted.
fieldNote: His **trial** includes paid time, actual materials and data permissions, rather than hiding the extra labour needed to repair errors.
He separates **personal income security** from concern about office colleagues whose household choices he cannot decide for them.

steps.text: Trial the AI parts-list tool on five jobs during paid work time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should try the useful bits instead of arguing about whether the whole trade is safe. Software could help the parts list and booking while we still do the actual tests. I'd want the trial measured in fewer wrong visits, not just more appointments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own paid hours to hold because practical work is still the bulk of the day. But I notice how much the office people do that the software is starting to offer. Even with my own income secure, I'd wonder what kind of firm we were becoming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask to trial the firm's AI parts-list tool on five ordinary jobs during paid work time. In the first year I'd compare its list with the materials actually used every month and show the crew the misses. I'd keep customer details out of any trial that wasn't approved for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about other people's jobs and the pressure to fit more visits in, but interested in the actual test. I don't feel my own bills are threatened. I'd like the firm to answer the staff question as carefully as the software question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk about the office jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager what changed for the staff before telling the staff what to do. Their work isn't an inconvenience to clear out of my way. A quicker parts list doesn't answer how someone pays the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a cheap-looking parts list repeatedly left things out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop using that part of the tool and show the missed item with the actual job record. I wouldn't make the crew collect missing materials in unpaid time so the trial looked successful. A result only counts if all the work is counted.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable robots around 2031 and use both preparation periods.
I'd keep trying tools without treating **physical skill** as a permanent hiding place from the same end point.
think: I expect **paid electrical hours** to shrink as firms bring in robots, with even strong skills offering no guarantee.
A **year of expenses** lets me try another route, without replacing decades of needed income.
do: Take **building-controls training** using at most one month's spare income from wages, preserving emergency savings.
Build a **practice board** using spare parts already owned.
Apply after 2028 for posted **service jobs** using completed training, checking written wages and hours before leaving.
feel: **Anxious** about falling income, with enough money and a practical plan to avoid feeling overwhelmed.
S2.quote: A year of expenses lets me try another route, but it can't fund the next thirty years.
fieldNote: His **training budget** comes from spare wage income, not rent money or emergency savings, and has a concrete spending cap.
He rejects **permanent protection** for controls work and treats completed skills plus actual vacancies as a possible next step.

steps.text: Take controls training within one month's spare wage income
Apply after 2028 for posted service jobs with checked wages and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to use the two years, not confuse them with the robot gap afterwards. Thinking work changes in 2028, and capable hands-on robots follow around 2031 in this picture. I'd keep testing new tools, but I'd stop calling physical skill a permanent hiding place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect fewer paid electrical hours as firms started bringing in robots, and that could reach me even with good skills. A year of expenses lets me try another route, but it can't fund the next thirty years. I'd have a lot of room to act and still worry about the income dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take an evening course in building-control testing, meaning checking the systems that run heating and lighting, using a capped amount from wages. I'd build a small practice board from spare parts I already own. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted service jobs using the completed course, comparing actual wages and hours before leaving the present job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a stronger urge to make something than to keep reading predictions. The money stops that urge becoming panic. It doesn't make the job loss I can imagine feel pleasant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could the course cost without weakening your reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cap the course spending at one month's normal spare income, not one month's living money. If the fee was higher, I'd find a cheaper provider or delay, and leave the year of expenses intact. I'd want practical teaching rather than a badge and a sales promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think controls work avoids the same eventual robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's a way to gain another useful skill while I'm still paid, not to escape the scenario's end point. Robots could reach controls work too. I'd check the actual vacancies instead of calling the course a guarantee.

say: I'd use **five years** for proper experiments instead of turning every course into an emergency purchase.
I'd keep the **2034 robot date** visible while checking choices rather than making confident guesses.
think: I expect several more years of **steady wages** before direct hands-on competition presses on my hours.
I can test whether **controls work pays** while still earning, without changing the eventual technology or my long career needs.
do: Complete **controls training** within the spare-wage spending cap and build a board from existing parts.
Ask to join paid **controls-testing jobs** before 2031, with experienced oversight for unfamiliar work.
Compare paid hours and **posted service jobs** quarterly after 2031, applying where written pay and schedules improve.
feel: **Uneasy** about the later career, while secure about near-term living and pleased to learn through paid practice.
S3.quote: A master licence doesn't mean I know every system already.
fieldNote: His **adaptability** includes seeking experienced oversight rather than equating fast learning with permission to guess on live customer work.
He treats **small experiments** as reversible and would inspect real vacancies instead of paying repeatedly to defend a disappointing course.

steps.text: Complete controls training within the spare-wage budget cap
Apply for posted service jobs when written pay and schedules improve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that five years lets us do proper experiments instead of turning the next course into an emergency purchase. I'd still keep the robot date around 2034 visible. More time should mean more checked choices, not more confident guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with the fast picture, I'd expect several more years of steady electrical wages before hands-on competition pressed on my hours. I could test whether controls work actually paid rather than rushing into it. The destination would still reach me young enough to need a long working future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take the controls course within the same cap from spare wages and build the practice board from existing parts. Before 2031 I'd ask to join paid controls-testing jobs at work. In the first year after 2031 I'd compare paid hours and posted service jobs every quarter, applying if another written wage and schedule were better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what my later career becomes, but secure about the next few years' living. I'd enjoy the chance to learn by doing while keeping my wage. I wouldn't mistake that enjoyable period for proof the robot end point had changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle unfamiliar controls work safely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask someone experienced to watch me test the practice board before I did unfamiliar work for a customer. Curiosity doesn't authorise me to guess with another person's wiring. A master licence doesn't mean I know every system already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course did not lead to paid work at your firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use the course as a small lesson rather than buy three more courses to defend the first decision. I'd look at actual vacancies and what they required. A failed small experiment is manageable with my reserve; an expensive story I refuse to question is worse.

say: I'd use **ten years** to revise the plan rather than force every experiment to become a business.
I'd judge learning by **useful paid work**, instead of counting tools tried or subscriptions bought.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I would still need working income after thinking AI and the later hands-on robots arrive.
High pay, a **year's reserve** and many local employers make my own living secure over the next few years.
do: Take practical **controls training** within the spare-wage cap and seek paid experience before further study.
Review **paid work gained** yearly against time and actual spending.
Apply after 2036 for better posted **service roles** if hours decline, keeping the present job until a signed offer.
feel: **Uneasy** about repeated career changes, but settled about present income and able to stop a poor trial.
S4.quote: The workbench isn't a company and the practice board isn't a customer order.
fieldNote: He rejects **assumed side income** from a hobby setup and names prerequisites without claiming he has started a business.
His **yearly review** tests actual paid work against spending, preserving a distinction between curiosity and an earning route.

steps.text: Take practical controls training within the spare-wage budget cap
Apply for better posted service roles if current paid hours decline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us room to change the plan several times. I'd keep experimenting but stop the idea that every experiment must become a business. We should measure what earns useful paid work, not how many new tools we've tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 at the thinking change in 2036 and around 40 when the robots followed. I don't need to solve every earning year now, but I can't call that retirement distance. With high trade pay, the reserve and plenty of local firms, I expect my own living to be secure over the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take the practical controls course within the spare-wage cap and seek paid experience before committing to further study. I'd review yearly whether the new skills brought actual work. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for better posted service roles if our hours declined, keeping the current wage until a signed offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about needing to change direction more than once, but settled about the next few years. I'd have time to stop a poor trial and start another. That's a much easier feeling than trying to be right before 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a business from the workbench now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't. The workbench isn't a company and the practice board isn't a customer order. I'd need real customers, permission from the employer and a costed plan before calling anything a business. I'm not taking those steps today just because there is a decade on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep experimentation useful over a whole decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record paid work gained, time spent and actual money used in a simple yearly sheet. If the sheet only showed new subscriptions, I'd stop buying them. A decade is enough time to change course, but also enough time to spend a fortune avoiding a decision.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could have to choose a new earning route before I've tested it properly. Practical courses with supervised work and clear vacancy information would help; I can cover a modest fee, but I can't buy proof that a course leads somewhere. My savings can pay for a mistake; I'd rather make a small one while I'm still earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what somebody stopped doing as well as what they started. I like new tools enough to keep a bad experiment alive because the next version looks exciting. Being able to stop is part of learning too.

headlineQuote: My savings can pay for a mistake; I'd rather make a small one while I'm still earning.
portrait: **Karl, 27**, leads electrical work with a technical diploma and master licence, earning high trade pay near many possible employers.
Single and childless, he has **a year's expenses** saved, uses checked AI daily and keeps a home workbench for experiments.
His **pragmatic curiosity** favours capped practical trials and supervised learning, without confusing hobby equipment with a business.
Fast competition threatens **paid hours** despite his resources; longer timelines allow paid practice and revision while near-term income remains secure.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could force a new earning decision before he has properly tested the route.
whatWouldHelp: Practical courses with **supervised work** would help him test useful skills.
Clear **vacancy information** would help distinguish a course from a real earning opportunity.
